rv.q: Dons will still dispute whether these two plays are one story but, in these performances, the argument is won.
An injection of stamping, torquing flamenco - and a bullfight - finesse Shakespeare’s wordy early comedy into something lusty and joyful here.
This production is, within its concept, generally a joy.
Lown-Collins’ production doesn’t really do much to combat these issues – the Latin is simply swapped for Spanish quips, and the ending is still the ending.
This labour of love doesn’t always pay off, then.
It works; but more clarity wouldn’t go amiss.
Stylish, sexy but strangely lacklustre, this shallow take on Shakespeare
The result, however, is a crude cacophony of impenetrable Spanish accents, punctuated by groin thrusts and clumsy pratfalls, with nothing to say about love, learning or loss.
This is a blazing, joyful triumph.
The advantage of staging one of Shakespeare’s lesser known plays is that it gives a director the liberty to put their own spin on it, no matter how outlandish.
What could have been a gimmick proves irresistible, with an abundance of creativity, energy, and heart.
This is a charming, intelligent evening of theatre that proves Shakespeare does not always need reinvention.

Overall, Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe is a vibrant summer production that successfully combines one of Shakespeare’s most challenging comedies with the passion and expressiveness of flamenco.
This creative approach is the best of both worlds.
The choreography, colour, and high spirits have the crowd fully on side.
This production is a triumph in each aspect and proves that reinvigorating Shakespeare’s works is entirely possible.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this flamenco-infused production, with most finding the Spanish concept bold and energetic, bringing fresh life to Shakespeare's tricky early comedy, though some feel the vibrant staging overwhelms the text.
